title: Acts 17:1–15
context: In Thessalonica Paul reasons from the Scriptures for three Sabbaths that the Christ had to suffer and rise, and some Jews and many God-fearing Greeks and leading women are persuaded. Jealous opponents form a mob, attack Jason’s house, and accuse the believers of turning the world upside down and proclaiming another king, Jesus. Sent to Berea, Paul finds Jews more noble-minded, who receive the word eagerly and examine the Scriptures daily, and many believe. When agitators arrive from Thessalonica, Paul is sent on to Athens.

verses.text: Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue.
verses.arminianNotes: They come to Thessalonica, where there is a synagogue. Arminian readers see Paul seeking out those who know the Scriptures.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the pattern of preaching to the Jew first.

verses.text: Paul, as was his custom, went in to them; and for three Sabbath days reasoned with them from the Scriptures,
verses.arminianNotes: For three Sabbaths Paul reasons with them from the Scriptures. Arminian commentators see persuasion addressed to the mind.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see Scripture as the ground of all gospel preaching.

verses.text: explaining and demonstrating that the Christ had to suffer and rise again from the dead, and saying, “This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.”
verses.arminianNotes: He explains that the Christ had to suffer and rise and that Jesus is the Christ. Arminian readers see reasoned proof offered for faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the necessity of the cross rooted in God’s plan.

verses.text: Some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas: of the devout Greeks a great multitude, and not a few of the chief women.
verses.arminianNotes: Some are persuaded and join Paul and Silas. Arminian expositors see persuasion leading to free decision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see God using persuasion as a means to bring his people to faith.

verses.text: But the unpersuaded Jews took along some wicked men from the marketplace and gathering a crowd, set the city in an uproar. Assaulting the house of Jason, they sought to bring them out to the people.
verses.arminianNotes: Unpersuaded Jews gather a mob and attack Jason’s house. Arminian readers see jealousy turning violent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see opposition following the word as before.

verses.text: When they didn’t find them, they dragged Jason and certain brothers before the rulers of the city, crying, “These who have turned the world upside down have come here also,
verses.arminianNotes: They drag Jason before the rulers, saying these men have turned the world upside down. Arminian commentators see an unintended compliment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see the gospel’s power to overturn the world’s order.

verses.text: whom Jason has received. These all act contrary to the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus!”
verses.arminianNotes: They claim the believers say there is another king, Jesus. Arminian readers see the political edge of confessing Christ as Lord.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Christ’s kingship over every earthly ruler.

verses.text: The multitude and the rulers of the city were troubled when they heard these things.
verses.arminianNotes: The crowd and rulers are disturbed. Arminian expositors see the gospel unsettling a city.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see God’s kingdom provoking the kingdoms of this world.

verses.text: When they had taken security from Jason and the rest, they let them go.
verses.arminianNotes: They take security from Jason and release them. Arminian readers see costly hospitality.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see believers sharing in the suffering of the messengers.

verses.text: The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Beroea. When they arrived, they went into the Jewish synagogue.
verses.arminianNotes: The brothers send Paul and Silas to Berea by night. Arminian commentators see prudence protecting the mission.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see providence opening a new door.

verses.text: Now these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.
verses.arminianNotes: The Bereans receive the word eagerly and examine the Scriptures daily. Arminian readers see open-minded inquiry as a model response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Scripture as the test of all teaching, even an apostle’s.

verses.text: Many of them therefore believed; also of the prominent Greek women, and not a few men.
verses.arminianNotes: Many of them believe, including prominent Greek women and men. Arminian expositors see careful study leading to faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed expositors see God blessing his word to many hearers.

verses.text: But when the Jews of Thessalonica had knowledge that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Beroea also, they came there likewise, agitating the multitudes.
verses.arminianNotes: Thessalonian Jews come to stir up the crowds in Berea. Arminian readers see opposition following the mission.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see persistent hostility that cannot stop the gospel.

verses.text: Then the brothers immediately sent out Paul to go as far as to the sea, and Silas and Timothy still stayed there.
verses.arminianNotes: The brothers send Paul to the coast while Silas and Timothy remain. Arminian commentators see the team adapting.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed commentators see God preserving both the messenger and the new church.

verses.text: But those who escorted Paul brought him as far as Athens. Receiving a commandment to Silas and Timothy that they should come to him very quickly, they departed.
verses.arminianNotes: Paul is escorted to Athens and sends for Silas and Timothy. Arminian readers see Paul alone in a new city.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God leading Paul to the intellectual center of the Greek world.
